Each rate is a small 2021 anchor carried forward by INE's Índice de Custos de Construção de Habitação Nova, which INE publishes monthly and splits into labour and materials — so a concrete pool and an imported lift escalate at their own rates rather than at one blended number.

Everything else is a ratio of one anchor: a standard build was about €1,000/m² in 2021, a concrete pool is 0.82 of the house rate per m² of water, a garage bay 0.55, a finished garden 0.041. Ratios do not go stale — what a pool costs relative to a house does not move with inflation, only the price of both does. Solar is the exception and is quoted flat: panels got cheaper since 2021 while building got dearer.

The headline carries a −15% / +25% band, deliberately lopsided: estimates of this kind miss low far more often than high, because scope grows, ground surprises you, and finishes get upgraded halfway through. It is a projection, not a quote.

Best fit is the most rooms a place usually sells for your budget, judged on what that typology typically costs there — not on the cheapest advert in it. One bargain T3 in Cascais does not make Cascais a place where €300,000 buys a T3. Places where the budget reaches nothing are left out rather than shown empty.

Min rooms turns the question from “where does my money buy something” into “where does it buy the T3 I actually need”, which has far fewer answers and is the one worth acting on. Stretch answers the question people really have at the edge of their means — and what would a little more get me. Places reached only by the stretch are marked stretch, never quietly mixed in with the ones that fit.

Click any row to see every typology the budget reaches there, not only the biggest. The headline answer assumes more rooms is what you want, and often it is not: the same money that reaches a small T3 also reaches a larger, cheaper-per-metre T2, and that trade is the actual decision.

The three number columns will not multiply out, and that is correct: each is its own middle value taken separately, and the middle price is not the middle size times the middle rate. Read each as “typically about this”, not as one worked example.

Deals is how many listings are asking at least 10% below what the valuation model thinks they are worth — under-priced, not cheap. A whole town being inexpensive is not a bargain; one flat below its own worth is. It sorts on the share, not the count, because 40 out of 2,000 is worse hunting than 8 out of 40.

A gap is the difference in median €/m² between two places close enough to be a real choice. This is where the money is: a border you cannot see on a price list.

Click any row to open it. These tables are wide, and reading a comparison across ten columns is the wrong shape for it — inside, the two places sit side by side with the listings behind each one, and the gap is worked out as money on a flat of the size that place actually sells. A rate per square metre is the honest way to compare two places and a useless way to picture the decision.

Distances are measured between the middle point of each place's listings, not between real borders — we hold no boundaries. So read 3 km as roughly how far you would move, not as an exact figure. Two places can also sit close on the map and still be separated by water or a motorway, which no distance here knows about.

Around one place shows every neighbour, including the ones priced much the same — “what is around Lisbon” means everything around it. Biggest gaps starts at a 20% floor instead, because every pair 1% apart across a whole level is thousands of rows of noise. Both floors live in Thresholds, and both can be changed.

Every place names itself with the places it sits inside underneath, and a chip saying which grain it is: a distrito is the broadest, a município is a council inside one, a freguesia is a parish inside that. Both halves of a pair are always the same grain — Level sets it, and it decides what counts as a neighbour at all.

Compare is the control that makes a gap trustworthy. On all stock, two places can sit 30% apart purely because one of them sells villas and the other sells studios — that gap is a fact about the buildings, not about the places, and moving would save you nothing. Pick a typology and it compares T2 against T2 instead. The all stock column stays on screen either way, because the two side by side are the real finding: “T2s are 30% apart while the places overall are within 4%” says something neither number says alone.

How the discount is worked out. Every listing in a place is sorted into one of three piles. A project is one whose advert says it needs work, or whose energy certificate is D or worse. Finished means the advert calls it good, renovated, or a new build. Everything else — an unknown condition with no certificate — goes in neither pile and is counted separately. The discount is the middle €/m² of the finished pile minus the middle €/m² of the project pile. That is the whole calculation: one subtraction between two medians, from real adverts.

Why the certificate does most of the work. “Needs renovation” is set on barely 1% of listings — too few for most places to have any project stock at all. A poor energy grade covers roughly ten times as many and is measured rather than typed by an agent. It is also not quite the same claim: a grade E flat is badly insulated, which overlaps with needing work without being identical to it. Open any row to see which of the two signals its projects came from.

Trust is why this screen is worth believing at all. Two medians always differ by something. Whether that something is a finding depends on how many adverts each side rests on, how far the two price spreads sit apart, and how much of the place's stock got sorted at all. Where the project prices and the finished prices cover the same ground, the gap between their middles is noise wearing a decimal point — and the row says so, with the reason.

Cost is an estimate, and yours to set. It is kept in its own column and never merged into the measured discount, because one is read off the market and the other is a guess — when the guess is wrong you need to be able to see it.

No place at level has both enough project stock and enough finished stock to compare. Lower Min listings, widen the area, or try a wider level — renovation stock is thin everywhere, which is exactly why the energy certificate is used to find it.

Pick a place, narrow it to one kind of property if you want. Every number is worked out from the listings at the moment you ask — no recalculation step to run first.

Median and average are both shown on purpose: the gap between them is the reading. They agree on an even market, and the average runs away from the median exactly where a few expensive listings are pulling it.

The distribution bars are as wide as the price range they cover, drawn between the 5th and the 95th percentile so one very expensive listing cannot stretch them until every other bar is empty — that listing is still counted, in the last bar.

Inside … is the section to read on a broad slice. A single median taken across every distrito describes no market you can buy in; the same listings split by place do. The split is always one grain finer than what you picked — distritos when nothing is narrowed, municípios inside a distrito, freguesias inside a município — and vs slice says how far each place sits from the median printed above it. Click any row to narrow the whole screen to that place.

Where a feature is worth wildly different amounts depending on the property — a sea view on the beachfront against one that means a sliver on the horizon — the row also shows what it reaches, and the conditions that figure holds under. Same model, different question: the headline stays the market-wide average.

Every number has a confidence range. Where that range crosses zero the data cannot tell whether the feature affects price at all — those rows say no measurable effect rather than showing a percentage, and sort to the bottom whichever column you sort on. Features whose ranges overlap cannot be ranked against each other. “Listings with it” is how many of the fitted listings actually carry the feature — the evidence behind that row, and why the rarer ones have wider ranges.
